Extended Rating Analysis

The main text reports six core exhibits: cost overview, human-vs-LLM scatter plot, agreement metrics, human baseline (Krippendorff’s alpha), criteria-level heatmap, and gap heatmap. The following extended analyses are preserved in the project’s git history and available in earlier rendered versions:

  • Krippendorff’s alpha by criterion: Inter-rater agreement treating human mean and each LLM as separate raters
  • CI coverage analysis: Share of human mean ratings falling within LLM 90% credible intervals
  • Bootstrap 95% CIs: Nonparametric confidence intervals for Pearson correlations
  • Mutual information: Information-theoretic measure of human-LLM rating dependence
  • Per-criterion correlations: Pearson and Spearman by evaluation criterion and model
  • Tier correlation dumbbell plot: How criteria predict journal tier judgments for humans vs. LLMs
  • Top disagreement cases: Papers with largest human-LLM rating differences
  • Prompt comparison: Legacy vs. updated GPT-5 Pro prompt effect on ratings

Extended Critique Analysis

The main text reports coverage-precision scatter and summary statistics. The following extended analyses are available in the full online version:

  • Paper-by-paper issue comparisons: Interactive collapsible panels showing matched issue pairs, unmatched human/LLM issues, and detailed discussion for each paper
  • Aggregate statistics: Total issue counts by severity, human vs. LLM issue distributions
  • Observable structural differences: Format, structure, attribution, and length comparisons
  • Manual annotation tool: Browser-based UI for systematic concordance labeling

This appendix presents detailed LLM evaluations for each paper, including:

  • Numerical ratings from all six models and human evaluators (where available)
  • Assessment summaries (collapsible) — the model’s written evaluation; available for all models including Claude Opus 4.6
  • Key issues (GPT-5.2 Pro only) — numbered list of methodological and evidential concerns
  • Reasoning traces (collapsible, GPT-5 Pro only) — internal reasoning process; not available for Claude Opus 4.6, which was run without extended thinking enabled (a re-run with thinking is planned)

The appendix is organized into two sections:

  1. Focal Papers — 14 papers evaluated with GPT-5.2 Pro using an extended prompt that produces structured key issues
  2. Other Papers — remaining papers with standard evaluations

  x,

  "adv_knowledge" = "Adv. Knowledge",

  .default = x
)

# Parse a single JSON response file
parse_paper_json <- function(path, model_name) {
  tryCatch({
    r <- jsonlite::fromJSON(path, simplifyVector = FALSE)

    # Extract parsed metrics (check r$parsed first, then output_text)
    parsed <- NULL
    if (!is.null(r$parsed) && length(r$parsed) > 0) {
      parsed <- r$parsed
    } else if (!is.null(r$output_text) && nchar(r$output_text) > 0) {
      txt <- r$output_text
      txt <- sub("^\\s*```[a-z]*\\s*\n?", "", txt)
      txt <- sub("\\s*```\\s*$", "", txt)
      parsed <- jsonlite::fromJSON(txt, simplifyVector = TRUE)
    } else if (!is.null(r$output)) {
      msg <- purrr::detect(r$output, ~ .x$type == "message", .default = NULL)
      if (!is.null(msg) && length(msg$content) > 0) {
        parsed <- jsonlite::fromJSON(msg$content[[1]]$text, simplifyVector = TRUE)
      }
    }

    # Extract metrics
    metrics_df <- NULL
    if (!is.null(parsed$metrics)) {
      rows <- list()
      for (nm in names(parsed$metrics)) {
        m <- parsed$metrics[[nm]]
        if (nm %in% c("tier_should", "tier_will", "journal_should", "journal_will")) {
          rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
            metric = nm,
            midpoint = m$score,
            lower = m$ci_lower,
            upper = m$ci_upper
          )
        } else {
          rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- tibble(
            metric = nm,
            midpoint = m$midpoint,
            lower = m$lower_bound,
            upper = m$upper_bound
          )
        }
      }
      metrics_df <- bind_rows(rows) |> mutate(model = model_name)
    }

    # Extract assessment summary
    assessment <- parsed$assessment_summary

    # Extract key_issues (GPT-5.2 Pro focal run only)
    key_issues <- NULL
    if (!is.null(parsed$key_issues) && length(parsed$key_issues) > 0) {
      key_issues <- parsed$key_issues
    }

    # Extract reasoning trace (GPT-5 Pro only)
    reasoning <- NA_character_
    if (!is.null(r$output)) {
      reasoning_block <- purrr::detect(r$output, ~ .x$type == "reasoning", .default = NULL)
      if (!is.null(reasoning_block) && !is.null(reasoning_block$summary)) {
        texts <- purrr::map_chr(reasoning_block$summary, ~ .x$text %||% "")
        reasoning <- paste(texts, collapse = "\n\n")
      }
    }

    list(
      metrics = metrics_df,
      assessment = assessment,
      key_issues = key_issues,
      reasoning = reasoning
    )
  }, error = function(e) {
    NULL
  })
}

# Load all LLM data for a specific paper
load_paper_llm_data <- function(paper_name) {
  all_metrics <- list()
  all_assessments <- list()
  all_key_issues <- list()
  reasoning <- NA_character_

  for (dir_name in names(MODEL_DIRS)) {
    model_name <- MODEL_DIRS[[dir_name]]

    # Try different filename formats
    json_dir <- here("results", dir_name, "json")
    if (!dir.exists(json_dir)) next

    # Look for matching file
    paper_clean <- str_replace_all(paper_name, " ", "_")
    possible_files <- c(
      file.path(json_dir, paste0(paper_name, ".response.json")),
      file.path(json_dir, paste0(paper_clean, ".response.json"))
    )

    path <- NULL
    for (pf in possible_files) {
      if (file.exists(pf)) {
        path <- pf
        break
      }
    }

    if (is.null(path)) next

    result <- parse_paper_json(path, model_name)
    if (!is.null(result)) {
      if (!is.null(result$metrics)) {
        all_metrics[[length(all_metrics) + 1]] <- result$metrics
      }
      if (!is.null(result$assessment) && !is.na(result$assessment)) {
        all_assessments[[model_name]] <- result$assessment
      }
      if (!is.null(result$key_issues) && length(result$key_issues) > 0) {
        all_key_issues[[model_name]] <- result$key_issues
      }
      if (!is.na(result$reasoning) && nchar(result$reasoning) > 0) {
        reasoning <- result$reasoning
      }
    }
  }

  list(
    metrics = if (length(all_metrics) > 0) bind_rows(all_metrics) else NULL,
    assessments = all_assessments,
    key_issues = all_key_issues,
    reasoning = reasoning
  )
}

# Load human data
load_human_ratings <- function() {
  rsx_path <- here("data", "rsx_evalr_rating.csv")
  if (!file.exists(rsx_path)) return(NULL)

  UJmap <- tryCatch(
    read.csv(here("data", "UJ_map.csv"), sep = ";", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(label_paper_title = research, label_paper = paper),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  rsx <- read.csv(rsx_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    janitor::clean_names() |>
    mutate(label_paper_title = research) |>
    select(-research)

  if (!is.null(UJmap)) {
    rsx <- rsx |>
      mutate(label_paper_title = str_trim(label_paper_title)) |>
      left_join(
        UJmap |> distinct(label_paper_title, label_paper),
        by = "label_paper_title",
        relationship = "many-to-one"
      )
  }

  rsx |>
    filter(!is.na(label_paper)) |>
    group_by(paper = label_paper, criteria) |>
    summarise(
      midpoint = mean(as.numeric(middle_rating), na.rm = TRUE),
      lower = mean(as.numeric(lower_ci), na.rm = TRUE),
      upper = mean(as.numeric(upper_ci), na.rm = TRUE),
      n_evals = n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      model = "Human",
      metric = criteria
    ) |>
    select(paper, model, metric, midpoint, lower, upper, n_evals)
}

human_ratings <- load_human_ratings()

# Get all unique papers across all model directories
get_all_papers <- function() {
  papers <- c()

  for (dir_name in names(MODEL_DIRS)) {
    json_dir <- here("results", dir_name, "json")
    if (!dir.exists(json_dir)) next

    files <- list.files(json_dir, pattern = "\\.response\\.json$", full.names = FALSE)
    paper_names <- files |>
      str_replace("\\.response\\.json$", "") |>
      str_replace_all("_", " ")

    papers <- c(papers, paper_names)
  }

  sort(unique(papers))
}

all_papers <- get_all_papers()
cat(sprintf("Found %d papers with LLM evaluations\n", length(all_papers)))
Found 60 papers with LLM evaluations

Focal Papers (GPT-5.2 Pro with Key Issues)

Acemoglu et al. 2024

NoteGPT-5 Pro Assessment

This paper investigates whether support for an entrenched authoritarian incumbent is sustained in part by voter misperceptions about democratic erosion and the benefits of democratic institutions, using a combined online survey experiment and a very large field experiment around Türkiye’s May 2023 elections. Strengths are substantial: both studies are preregistered/IRB-approved; the online experiment includes carefully designed placebo texts to diagnose experimenter demand; the field experiment randomizes at the neighborhood level across more than half a million voters, uses administrative ballot-box outcomes (presidential first and second rounds, parliamentary election, and one-year-later municipal election), and instruments treatment intensity (share of completed canvassing interactions) with randomized assignment. Estimated impacts are consistent across modalities: information correcting misperceptions about media independence/democracy and their real-world implications increases beliefs aligned with research and V-Dem trends, raises opposition voting intentions online by ~3.7 pp (with near-zero placebo effects), and increases opposition vote shares in the field by ~2.4 pp (no turnout effects). Heterogeneity patterns also align with the core mechanism: larger effects among individuals/neighborhoods ex ante more misinformed or leaning toward the incumbent, and higher effects when canvassers are non-affiliated rather than opposition party affiliates, supporting a credibility channel. The analysis is clearly written, with transparent estimation, strong first stages, balance checks, consistency across alternative control sets and alternative endogenous treatment measures (completed vs initiated conversations or pamphlet drop-offs), and reduced-form estimates reported. Several issues merit careful consideration. (1) Identification and interpretation. The field experiment necessarily lacks an individual-level post-treatment survey (the authors attempted and failed to collect follow-up), so mechanisms linking belief updating to ballot outcomes cannot be established within the same subjects; the mechanism is inferred from the online experiment and neighborhood-level heterogeneity in the field. This triangulation is reasonable but should be framed as “consistent with,” not definitive. Moreover, the field “basic” message contains slogans and a call to action, and the CHP/İYİ pamphlets contain partisan branding, creating a bundle of information plus mobilizing/partisan cues. The “high-credibility” variant is closer to non-partisan facts, but still includes, in party-affiliated arms, party imagery that could weaken the claim of neutral information. The authors mitigate this with non-affiliated canvasser arms and by showing no turnout effects, yet some persuasion could still operate via motivational priming rather than pure belief correction. The authors appropriately present results for high-credibility and basic treatments separately, but the main headline effects are often presented in a bundled fashion; more emphasis on the unbundled contrasts and on non-affiliated effects would isolate the information channel further. (2) External validity and timing. Izmir is an opposition-leaning province; while effects concentrate in neighborhoods that were previously less favorable to the opposition, generalizing to other provinces or countries with different repression/propaganda equilibria is uncertain. The salience of the catastrophic 2023 earthquake and corruption concerns plausibly amplify treatment potency; this context-dependence is a feature but limits generalization. (3) SUTVA/spillovers. Neighborhood-level randomization with door-to-door canvassing risks contamination if treated messages diffuse into adjacent control neighborhoods through social networks or canvasser routing. The protocols geocode and route canvassers, but the paper does not present explicit spatial spillover checks (e.g., outcomes by distance to treated neighborhoods or exclusion buffers). If spillovers exist, ITT estimates could be attenuated; however, in principle they could also bias results if spillovers are asymmetric. (4) Treatment measurement and fidelity. The endogenous regressor is the share of completed conversations from canvasser logs; self-reported logs may have reporting error. The authors address this via instrumental variables, present strong first stages, and show robustness using initiated conversations and pamphlet drops. Still, fidelity audits (spot checks, audio capture, or independent observers) would further bolster confidence that treatment delivery was uniform across canvasser types and treatments. (5) Estimation presentation. The field results emphasize 2SLS LATE/TOT magnitudes (~2.4 pp); these are well complemented by reduced form (~0.8 pp), but readers may conflate the two. The figures clearly note 2SLS; still, consistently pairing TOT with RF in the main text would avoid misinterpretation. (6) Outcome multiplicity and adjustments. The paper examines multiple outcomes (beliefs, intentions, three 2023 races, turnout, 2024 municipal election) and heterogeneity dimensions. The strongest results have very small p-values and replicate across settings, mitigating multiple-testing concerns, but no formal adjustment is reported. (7) Foundations of factual claims. The paper treats V-Dem’s indices as ground truth for democracy/media decline, and the informational prompts rely on research summarizing relationships between democracy/media and outcomes (disaster mortality, corruption). These are reasonable choices and widely used, but there is measurement and causal identification debate in the literatures. The authors present these as “according to research” and cite canonical studies; providing sensitivity to alternative indices (e.g., FH, Polity) in the online prompt or additional figures in the appendix would defuse claims that the information is contestable. (8) Placebos and demand effects in the field. Because outcomes are administrative vote shares, experimenter demand is unlikely; still, the lack of a field placebo arm leaves open whether any pro-opposition contact could drive similar effects. The lack of turnout changes and the credibility gradient by canvasser affiliation partially mitigate this, but a cluster-randomized placebo with non-political content would be a valuable addition. (9) Long-run effects. The one-year municipal effect is marginally significant and small; given intervening events, it should be interpreted cautiously (though randomization helps), and power calculations for long-run effects are not presented. (10) Sampling and exclusion. The field sample excludes remote neighborhoods requiring more time to canvass; this is operationally reasonable but limits representativeness within Izmir. For the online experiment, Facebook-recruited respondents are not representative, and attrition is non-trivial (though balanced). The authors are transparent about both points and use the online component primarily for mechanisms and belief updating. (11) Ethics and risk. The paper reports dual IRB approvals and registry, and indicates a non-partisan invitation to all major parties. The non-partisan arm is a strength, though the governing parties’ refusal to participate constrains balance across affiliations. Overall, the design, execution, and triangulation between online and field evidence are strong. The central claims are well supported within the caveats above: voters systematically misperceive democratic erosion and the value of democracy/media; credible, accurate information reduces misperceptions and shifts vote choices toward opposition; effects are concentrated among the misinformed and incumbent-leaning; and credibility/non-partisanship matters. The paper meaningfully advances empirical understanding of persuasion under authoritarianism and offers practical lessons for civic communication strategies. Replication is feasible in principle (administrative outcomes, clear estimators, and randomization), but would benefit from full code release, canvasser logs, and treatment materials in a public repository alongside the registry.

NoteGPT-5.2 Pro Assessment

This manuscript studies whether support for an increasingly authoritarian incumbent can partly reflect misperceptions about (i) the extent of democratic and media erosion and (ii) the practical value of democracy/media freedom for salient outcomes, rather than a genuine preference for authoritarianism. It combines (a) an online survey experiment recruited via Facebook ads (with placebo “demand” messages) and (b) a large neighborhood-randomized door-to-door canvassing field experiment in one major city, linked to administrative ballot-box election returns. The core empirical results—information shifts beliefs and increases opposition vote intention/actual opposition vote share by roughly 2–4 pp—are internally coherent across the two experiments and are strengthened by the field study’s use of administrative outcomes (reducing concerns about experimenter demand or social desirability in the main endpoint). The paper is also unusually transparent about design choices (registration, IRB, stratification, rerandomization, canvasser identity cross-randomization) and conducts a set of sensible robustness checks (controls, alternative “contact” measures, reduced form vs IV, heterogeneous effects patterns that align with their mechanism story). Nevertheless, several issues in the manuscript materially affect interpretability and generalization. First, the core construct “misperception” is defined relative to V-Dem indices treated as ground truth; while V-Dem is a high-quality expert-coded dataset, it is not direct “official data” and is not an unambiguous truth benchmark for citizens’ beliefs. The treatment scripts and pamphlets sometimes label these indicators as “official data,” which risks overstating epistemic certainty and could itself affect credibility and persuasion; this matters because the paper’s conceptual claim hinges on “accurate information correcting misperceptions.” Relatedly, the causal claims embedded in the informational scripts (“as democracy strengthens, deaths/building damage from disasters decrease”; “as media independence worsens, corruption increases”) are presented in a strongly causal way, but the cited evidence is largely observational/cross-country (and context dependent). Even if the literature supports an average association, presenting it as a simple law may be contestable; if respondents update because they perceive a broad normative/valence message (or because they view the intervention as an opposition argument packaged as science), the interpretation “beliefs corrected by accuracy” becomes less clean.

Second, the field experiment’s treatment content and delivery raise identification and interpretation questions about what exactly is being estimated. The “high-credibility” pamphlet is closer to factual claims, but it is still an opposition-aligned valence message in a highly polarized campaign environment; the “basic” pamphlet is explicitly mobilizational and, in versions shown, includes candidate/party branding. The paper emphasizes non-partisanship in approach, but the realized intervention was implemented with opposition parties and included overt opposition branding in at least some arms. This complicates the interpretation that the effect is driven primarily by informational correction rather than standard partisan persuasion/mobilization channels (even if turnout does not change). In addition, the paper’s preferred field estimates are 2SLS effects of “completed conversations” instrumented by neighborhood assignment. This is reasonable as a compliance-adjusted estimand, but the exclusion restriction is not fully innocuous: assignment affects not only conversation completion but also pamphlet exposure, canvasser presence, perceived campaign intensity, and possibly social spillovers within neighborhoods. The authors do show reduced forms and alternative endogenous variables (initiated conversations, pamphlets left), which helps, but the narrative sometimes slides from an IV-LATE per conversation to a broader claim about “information” effects. Interference/spillovers are plausible (adjacent neighborhoods, within-building networks, media/social discussion) and could bias reduced-form effects toward zero or alter interpretation; the paper does not deeply model or bound spillovers.

Third, external validity is limited in ways that deserve more emphasis. The field experiment occurs in one province/city with distinctive political composition (often described as an opposition stronghold), and neighborhood sampling excludes remote/time-costly areas. The mechanism claims about persuading incumbent supporters are supported by stronger effects in “below-median opposition share” neighborhoods, but this is a within-city comparison and may not transport to national contexts, rural settings, or places with different media ecosystems/repression. Likewise, the online experiment is recruited via Facebook ads, with a sizable drop-off from clickers to completers and a lottery-like incentive; even with balance/attrition checks, representativeness is weak, and the degree to which online respondents resemble marginal persuadables in the electorate is uncertain. The paper generally treats the online experiment as mechanism-support (belief updating, placebo check) and the field experiment as the main outcome test, which is appropriate, but readers may still overgeneralize.

Fourth, some measurement/integrity details merit clarification. In the appendix summary statistics, turnout in administrative data exceeds 1 in some ballot boxes (e.g., max 1.16), which is not impossible in some administrative systems (e.g., list updates, ballot box reassignment, denominator mismatch), but it requires explicit explanation because it can signal mismatched denominators or merging issues. In the online study, there is a potential inconsistency in the definition of the “Turnout” variable (appendix definition appears inverted relative to how it is used in figures/means), which could be a documentation error but should be resolved for replicability. Additionally, the “placebo” scripts still contain substantive propositions (“some people think media independence worsened and corruption increased”), which may not be a pure demand-only placebo; if anything, this makes the placebo a weak-information condition, complicating the interpretation that placebo effects isolate demand.

Finally, the heterogeneity and longer-term persistence results are intriguing but should be treated cautiously. Many subgroup analyses are median splits and may not all be pre-registered; multiple testing and researcher degrees of freedom could inflate apparent structure. The municipal-election effect a year later is potentially important, but persistence claims need more discussion of competing explanations (differential subsequent campaigning, migration, compositional changes of ballot boxes, or correlated neighborhood trends) and of how stable ballot-box mapping is across elections (the paper notes ballot boxes cannot be tracked over time in some contexts). Overall, the manuscript provides strong experimental evidence that credible-sounding institutional-performance information can move beliefs and election outcomes at the margin under competitive authoritarian conditions, but the conceptual leap from “information treatment” to “correction of misperceptions about true institutional state/causal impacts” is somewhat overstated, and the field implementation’s partisan entanglement and possible interference limit how cleanly one can attribute the effect to neutral information per se.

NoteClaude Opus 4.6 Assessment

This paper investigates whether misperceptions about democracy and media freedom contribute to support for authoritarian regimes, using Türkiye’s May 2023 elections as a case study. The authors conduct both an online experiment (N≈4,400) and a large-scale field experiment (≈880,000 voters in Izmir) providing accurate information about the deterioration of democratic institutions and media freedom under AKP rule, and their implications for natural disaster preparedness and corruption. The key findings are that informational treatments increase opposition vote share by 3.7 percentage points online and 2.4 percentage points in the field, with effects concentrated among government supporters and those with greater misperceptions.

Strengths: (1) The combination of an online experiment with a large-scale field experiment using administrative voting data is a major methodological strength. The online experiment allows measurement of belief changes and includes a placebo treatment to control for experimenter demand effects, while the field experiment provides hard behavioral outcomes immune to self-report bias. (2) The heterogeneity analysis is compelling and consistent across both experiments—effects are driven by those with greater misperceptions and by neighborhoods leaning toward the government, not by opposition mobilization. This is crucial for the paper’s interpretation. (3) The pre-registration, balance checks, and extensive robustness analyses (varying controls, endogenous variable definitions, etc.) enhance credibility. (4) The research question is of first-order importance for understanding democratic backsliding globally.

Concerns and limitations: (1) The field experiment was conducted only in Izmir, Türkiye’s third-largest city and a known opposition stronghold. This limits external validity—effects might differ substantially in government strongholds where misperceptions may be deeper but also where social pressure against opposition voting may be stronger. The authors acknowledge this implicitly through their heterogeneity analysis but do not discuss this limitation extensively. (2) The field experiment partnered with opposition parties (CHP and İYİ) after governing coalition parties declined participation. While the authors tried to maintain non-partisan framing in the high-credibility treatment, the basic informational treatment contained explicitly partisan language (‘Let’s protect democracy together,’ calls to action). The bundling of these two treatments for the main results makes it harder to isolate the effect of pure information provision from partisan mobilization. The fact that the two treatment effects are statistically indistinguishable somewhat undermines the clean ‘misperception correction’ interpretation. (3) The online sample was recruited via Facebook ads, raising concerns about representativeness. The sample skews male (80%) and politically engaged, which may not reflect the broader Turkish electorate. (4) The 35% completion rate in the field experiment means that many treated households received only a pamphlet left at the door. The 2SLS approach addresses this, but the resulting estimates reflect the effect on compliers, which may differ from the average voter. (5) The characterization of government supporters’ beliefs as ‘misperceptions’ relies on V-DEM data as ground truth. While V-DEM is widely respected, government supporters might reasonably contest its assessments. The paper could benefit from acknowledging this epistemological issue more carefully. (6) The 2024 municipal election effects (Panel C of Figure 4) are described as showing persistence, but these elections occurred in a very different political context (CHP won major cities including Istanbul), making it difficult to attribute the effect purely to the earlier treatment. (7) The online experiment shows some pre-treatment imbalances (Table A-3), and while robustness checks are provided, the relatively small sample size means precision depends on controlling for these. (8) The paper does not fully address potential spillover effects within neighborhoods in the field experiment—treated households may have shared information with untreated households, which could bias estimates. (9) The interpretation that effects persist through the 2024 elections is interesting but speculative—many intervening events could explain voting pattern changes. (10) The paper could more carefully discuss the welfare implications of the information provision—whether reducing misperceptions necessarily improves democratic outcomes depends on assumptions about what constitutes accurate information about institutional quality.

NoteGemini 2.0 Flash Assessment

This paper investigates the impact of providing information about the state of democracy and media freedom on voter behavior in Turkey. The authors conducted both an online experiment and a field experiment in Izmir during the lead-up to the May 2023 elections. The online experiment involved exposing participants to information about the decline of democracy and media freedom, as well as their importance in addressing issues like natural disasters and corruption. The field experiment involved door-to-door canvassing in select neighborhoods of Izmir, where residents received similar information. The key finding is that providing information increased support for the opposition, particularly among voters who were initially more supportive of the incumbent government and held misperceptions about the state of democratic institutions. This suggests that at least some support for authoritarian regimes comes from misperceptions rather than inherent preferences. The authors conclude that providing accurate information can bridge ideological divides and sway voters. They also find that the source of information matters, with non-affiliated canvassers being more effective than those affiliated with opposition parties.

Several issues arise upon review. First, there is the question of external validity. The study focuses on Turkey, a country with specific political and social dynamics. It is unclear how well these findings would generalize to other countries with different contexts. The authors acknowledge this to some extent but do not fully explore the limitations. Second, there are potential issues with experimenter demand effects in the online experiment. While the authors include placebo treatments, it’s still possible that participants altered their responses to align with what they believed the researchers wanted to see. The authors acknowledge this limitation and argue that the field experiment, which relies on actual voting behavior, helps to mitigate this concern.

Third, there are questions about the robustness of the findings to different specifications and control variables. The authors address this to some extent by presenting results with different sets of controls, but it’s still possible that other factors could be driving the results. Fourth, there may be limitations in the field experiment due to the non-random assignment of treatments at the individual level. Instead, treatment was assigned at the neighborhood level, potentially leading to spillover effects and other forms of interference. The authors acknowledge that this may lead to varying proportions of treated households. Fifth, the authors state that the governing coalition parties did not accept to take part in their study and they were therefore unable to assess how the information campaign impacted their supporters. It may be that the information shared had limited reach to these voters or was ignored because of its source.

Sixth, it is not clear how the information being shared was regarded by citizens in light of propaganda and misinformation. It could be that any information shared by any party or group would be disregarded completely as being untrustworthy. Seventh, the door-to-door information campaign was implemented in Izmir, Turkey’s third-largest province. The extent to which this can be generalized to the rest of Turkey, including more rural areas is not clear. Eight, the basic informational treatment used in the field experiment contained less impartial and more partisan language which calls into question whether citizens viewed the experiment as unbiased. Overall, these issues somewhat temper the positive findings of the research.

NoteGPT-5 Pro Assessment

This manuscript reports a large-scale, geo-randomized natural field experiment testing whether Facebook video fundraising increases charitable giving. Roughly 7,686 German postal codes (after excluding extreme Facebook-reach PLZs) were assigned in blocks to either a 14-day Save the Children video campaign or to pure control, with a 2×2 factorial variation in video content (empathy vs. effectiveness) and impression allocation strategy (Facebook free allocation vs. fixed postal-code budgets proportional to estimated potential × reach). Outcomes are daily donation revenue and counts to Save the Children at the PLZ-day level, aggregated across all donation channels (online and offline), over 31 pre-treatment days, 14 treatment days, and 38 post-treatment days (with some checks extending into early January). The study additionally leverages two external datasets of donations to other charities (a 23-charity alliance and betterplace.org projects) to assess competitive spillovers, and presents several robustness checks, including difference-in-differences, randomization inference, and sensitivity to post-campaign window length. The central findings are: (i) significant increases in donation frequency both during and (especially) over the combined during+post period; (ii) a positive effect on revenue that is marginally significant in the long-term window, with point estimates implying immediate profitability (≈€1.45 per €1 spent) and higher long-run returns under a lifetime value assumption; (iii) evidence of crowding out of other children-related or similar charities/projects; (iv) little long-run difference between empathy and effectiveness content despite stronger short-run attention and clicks for the empathy video; (v) limited performance differences between free and fixed impression allocation (with some short-run advantages for free allocation); and (vi) local spillovers to neighboring PLZs suggesting interference (thus main effects are lower bounds on total impact).

Most important issues and limitations: - Identification and pre-trends: For Save the Children outcomes, pretreatment differences across treatment/control PLZs are small and statistically insignificant, and the preferred specifications include the lagged dependent variable and block fixed effects. For the alliance data, pretreatment differences are significant; the paper appropriately relies on controls and difference-in-differences estimators. While randomization should ensure unbiasedness, the presence of pretreatment imbalances in some auxiliary datasets raises residual concerns about time-varying shocks or regression-to-the-mean effects. The paper provides randomization inference and robustness checks which help, but an explicit pre-registered primary analysis for competition outcomes and a systematic treatment of multiplicity would strengthen inference. - Interference and spillovers: The authors document positive spillovers from treated nearby PLZs (≤30 km), especially from urban neighbors and affecting rural areas more, implying violations of SUTVA and that ITT estimates are lower bounds on total effects. Their post-hoc adjustment using the share of treated neighbors offers a useful diagnostic but is necessarily model-based and not pre-registered; the magnitude and interpretation of “total effects” remain somewhat sensitive to specification. A design explicitly accommodating network/geo spillovers or two-stage randomization would sharpen these estimates. - Exposure and dosage: In the “free allocation” arm, the platform endogenously varied impressions across treated PLZs, creating meaningful heterogeneity in treatment intensity. Analyses are reported at the ITT level; the paper does not instrument for dosage or present dose-response analyses at PLZ level (impressions per capita), which could clarify mechanisms and effect heterogeneity. The factorial variation (free vs. fixed allocation) partly addresses this, but a complier- or intensity-based analysis would be valuable. - Profitability and long-run impact: The ROI calculations extrapolate from the long-run point estimate with wide confidence intervals and employ an assumed donor lifetime value (LTV = 1.75) and persistence figures drawn from prior work/industry norms, not estimated directly on ad-acquired donors. This is reasonable for a managerial back-of-the-envelope but introduces uncertainty; retention and average gift sizes could differ for ad-acquired donors versus incumbents. The paper correctly flags the uncertainty but could further explore plausible ranges and scenario analyses. - Competition and net sector effects: The paper provides valuable evidence of crowding out using two non-overlapping-but-not-disjoint data sources (an alliance of 23 charities and betterplace.org). However, both are online-only (whereas Save the Children outcomes include all channels), making it hard to infer full general equilibrium effects across the sector. Overlap between the data sources, missing offline donations for competitors, and significant pretreatment differences in the alliance data complicate any precise estimate of net sectoral welfare. The direction (crowding out) is reasonably supported; the magnitude remains uncertain. - Measurement and aggregation: Outcomes are aggregated at the PLZ-day level and winsorized at €1,000 on PLZ-day observations (68 affected). The authors report that results are robust without winsorization but with less precision; still, winsorization at the PLZ-day level, rather than donor-level, is a pragmatic compromise that could slightly affect distributional inferences. Normalizing per-million-inhabitants-per-day and then scaling to treated population is clear; reporting both per-capita ATE and population-weighted totals is appropriate. The lack of an individual-level click-to-donation linkage (especially under free allocation where click data are semi-aggregated by group) limits mechanistic interpretation when contrasting intermediate metrics with eventual donations. - Pre-registration and analytic flexibility: The design was preregistered, but the blocking variable set was expanded (to include Facebook reach) and the impression allocation strategy arm was added post registration. The core main effects analysis aligns with the experimental design, but multiple secondary analyses (heterogeneity, spillovers, competition, and intermediate metrics) are extensive. A formal multiplicity adjustment is not presented; readers should interpret marginal p-values with caution. - External validity: The setting is Germany in November–December (peak giving season) with Save the Children, a large, well-known charity, and a largely untargeted campaign. This maximizes policy relevance for general audiences and non-targeted campaigns but may not generalize to less salient charities, non-seasonal periods, different geographies, or more targeted/different ad channels. The authors’ heterogeneity results suggest that targeting higher-potential PLZs would likely improve ROI materially. - Open science and replicability: The study leverages proprietary donation data and platform metrics; data are aggregated and anonymized, and not public. The experiment was preregistered and the online appendix is detailed, but no analysis code or replication package appears to be provided. Reproducibility by third parties is therefore limited without data access, although the methodological descriptions are sufficiently clear to permit re-implementation given similar data.

Overall, the design is strong: large-scale randomization, outcomes covering all donation channels for the focal charity, a meaningful post-campaign horizon, attention to spillovers, and careful discussion of substitution versus expansion. The principal limitations concern interference (and the resulting interpretation of ITT as a lower bound), incomplete sector coverage for competition outcomes (and channel mismatch), reliance on assumed LTV for profitability, and limited replicability due to proprietary data. The claims are generally well-calibrated to the evidence: the increase in donation frequency is robust; the revenue effect is positive but only marginally significant; profitability is plausible but uncertain; and click-based intermediate metrics can be misleading relative to long-run donations. The paper provides practically useful guidance to fundraisers and a valuable contribution to the economics of charitable giving and digital advertising, with particularly useful insights on general equilibrium effects and on the (limited) inferential value of engagement metrics for ultimate fundraising outcomes.

NoteGPT-5.2 Pro Assessment

This manuscript studies whether Facebook video fundraising increases charitable giving using a large geo-randomized field experiment across 7,686 German postal codes, linking treatment assignment to the full universe of the focal charity’s donations at the postal-code-by-day level and (partially) to donations to other charities/projects. The design is unusually ambitious and well-motivated: by randomizing at geography and measuring total donations rather than click-through conversions, it directly targets common advertising-evaluation problems (channel substitution, untracked delayed/offline conversions, and low power from rare individual-level donation events). The main identification argument—treated and control postal codes are comparable due to block randomization, so differences in donation outcomes during/after the campaign can be attributed to the ads—is plausible, supported by balance checks, and strengthened by randomization-inference robustness. However, several internal threats and interpretive risks remain. First, interference/spillovers are likely in geo experiments with platform targeting (misclassification of location, commuting, and cross-area social exposure); the paper finds positive “treated neighbors” associations and interprets them as spillovers implying lower-bound direct effects, but this spillover analysis is not itself experimentally manipulated, and the “share treated within 30km” is mechanically correlated with many spatial features and with block structure; thus it is suggestive but not definitive evidence about interference magnitude or direction. Given potential interference, conventional SUTVA-based estimands are ambiguous: the reported treatment effect is closer to an “assignment-to-treatment intensity” effect under partial interference rather than a clean individual exposure effect, and the paper’s conversion of coefficients into campaign-level profit implicitly assumes a particular mapping from assignment to exposure that may not hold if spillovers are material. Second, the mapping from postal-code assignment to actual impression delivery is only partially observed and is mediated by Facebook’s delivery algorithm; while the paper reports aggregate reach/impressions and a factorial manipulation of allocation strategy, there is still substantial scope for differential delivery within treated postal codes (e.g., toward cheaper-to-reach users) that could create heterogeneous treatment intensity unrelated to charitable propensity, complicating interpretation as a per-capita causal effect. Third, statistical strength differs across outcomes: donation frequency effects are consistently significant, but donation revenue effects are weaker (long-term revenue significant only at p<0.1 in the preferred specification), making the profitability conclusion sensitive to functional-form assumptions and tail behavior. The paper addresses outliers via winsorization at €1,000 at the PLZ-day level; while it reports similar point estimates without winsorization, inference and ROI can still be sensitive because the revenue effect is borderline and charitable gifts are heavy-tailed. Also, the main outcome construction aggregates into three periods and scales “per million inhabitants per day,” which is sensible for comparability but obscures dynamic treatment effects and makes the choice of post period (ending Dec 31) consequential; the justification is that effects should fade after the fiscal-year giving season, yet this choice intertwines treatment persistence with strong seasonality, and the “sensitivity to days included” figure helps but does not fully resolve whether the late-December revenue uptick is treatment-driven or a differential seasonal pattern that remains by chance in treated areas. Fourth, competition/crowding-out results are valuable but less clean: for the alliance of 23 charities the authors find pretreatment imbalance and therefore rely on lagged-outcome controls and DiD-style changes. These approaches are reasonable, but the outcomes differ in scope (only online giving for competitors vs all channels for the focal charity), overlap between datasets is acknowledged but unresolved, and the analysis cannot measure total sector-wide giving; therefore the welfare/sector conclusion (“redistribution/lost to the sector”) remains speculative. For the donation platform data, category tagging and the project-level aggregation introduce classification and compositional issues (projects vs organizations; multiple tags) that can attenuate or misattribute substitution. Fifth, the 2×2 factorial “mechanism” claims are cautiously worded but still at risk of over-interpretation: video-type differences in donations are mostly not statistically distinguishable, while intermediate metrics (views/clicks) differ strongly; this supports the managerial point that clicks are poor proxies for donations, but the paper’s broader inference (“power of asking” is main mechanism) is not directly tested against alternative mechanisms (mere salience, trust signals, or contemporaneous external events). Sixth, the heterogeneity exercise reports many interactions and suggests targeting improvements; these are likely exploratory (and appear not fully preregistered), raising multiplicity and overfitting concerns, especially because the blocking procedure itself used a prediction model based on past donations and covariates, which can interact with subsequent heterogeneity patterns. Finally, open-science and reproducibility are mixed: preregistration is a major strength and the appendix is extensive, but key inputs (donation microdata, competitor data, platform delivery logs) are proprietary/partially aggregated, and it is unclear whether replication code and complete analysis scripts are available; this limits independent verification of data processing decisions (winsorization, aggregation, population scaling, neighbor calculations) and of exact specification search. Overall, the paper’s central empirical contribution—a large-scale, plausibly causal estimate of incremental donations from Facebook fundraising with evidence of some substitution across charities—is credible and useful, but several conclusions (especially profitability magnitude, spillover-adjusted “total effects,” and sector-level implications) should be treated as more uncertain and assumption-dependent than the main narrative sometimes suggests.

NoteClaude Opus 4.6 Assessment

This paper examines whether online fundraising via Facebook video ads increases charitable giving, using a geo-randomized field experiment covering nearly 8,000 German postal codes. The study represents a well-designed and carefully executed natural field experiment that addresses several important limitations of prior work on online fundraising effectiveness, particularly channel substitution, intertemporal substitution, and measurement issues inherent in click-through data. The design is preregistered and uses blocking with machine learning to ensure balance.

Key strengths: (1) The geo-randomized design is innovative and well-suited to the research question. By randomizing at the postal code level and measuring total donations across all channels, the authors avoid the common pitfall of only measuring donations through the advertised link. (2) The scale is impressive—nearly all German postal codes over 12 weeks—providing substantial external validity. (3) The 2x2 factorial design (empathy vs. effectiveness video; free vs. fixed budget allocation) adds valuable secondary findings. (4) The analysis of competition effects using two independent data sources on rival charities is a genuine contribution. (5) The study is preregistered and the authors are transparent about deviations. (6) The robustness checks, including randomization inference and sensitivity to post-campaign window length, are thorough.

Key concerns and limitations: (1) Statistical power for the donation revenue outcome remains limited. The main revenue effect is only significant at p<0.1 in the long-term specification, which is marginal. The short-term revenue effect is not statistically significant. This is acknowledged but deserves more emphasis—the confidence intervals are extremely wide (90% CI for long-term return per euro spent: 0.15–2.74), making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about profitability. (2) The competition/crowding-out results are suggestive but also imprecisely estimated and rely on datasets with pretreatment imbalances (the 23-charity alliance data). The pretreatment imbalance in the competition data (Table A4 shows significant differences) is a concern, even though DiD specifications are used to address it. The crowding-out magnitudes appear potentially larger than the Save the Children gains, which the authors note but do not fully reconcile—this raises questions about whether the campaign created net social value. (3) The lifetime value (LTV) multiplier of 1.75 used in the profitability calculation is based on assumptions drawn from other contexts and industry benchmarks rather than directly observed data. The profitability conclusion is quite sensitive to this assumption. (4) The spillover analysis (Table 8) adds a variable for share of treated neighbors, but this variable is not randomly assigned—it is endogenous to the blocking structure. The interpretation of these coefficients as causal spillover effects requires caution. (5) There are some deviations from the preregistered design (footnote 13 mentions adding the reach variable to blocking and adding the second treatment dimension), though these are disclosed. (6) The paper does not provide individual-level data or code, and the appendix is hosted separately as a URL rather than being included. The online appendix link may not be permanently accessible. (7) The winsorization at €1,000 at the PLZ-day level rather than the individual level is noted as a limitation but could affect results given 68 affected observations. (8) The experiment was conducted in 2017, and the Facebook advertising ecosystem has evolved considerably since then, potentially limiting the current relevance of the specific magnitudes.

On the competition effects, the finding of crowding out from similar charities is important and novel in this experimental context, but the evidence is mixed across specifications and data sources. The betterplace.org analysis shows a significant negative interaction for children-related projects in the short term (Table 4) but not in the long term. The 23-charity alliance results are significant only in the DiD specification. The paper appropriately characterizes these as suggestive evidence.

The paper’s practical recommendation—that click-through data may be misleading for evaluating fundraising campaigns—is well-supported by the divergent patterns between intermediate metrics (clicks, watch time) and actual donation outcomes. This is a valuable insight for practitioners.

Overall, this is a high-quality field experiment with a creative design that advances our understanding of online fundraising effectiveness. The main limitation is the precision of the revenue estimates, which are economically meaningful but statistically borderline. The paper is well-written, clearly organized, and honest about its limitations.

NoteGemini 2.0 Flash Assessment

This paper investigates the effect of online fundraising on charitable giving using a geo-randomized field experiment on Facebook. The authors partnered with Save the Children and randomly assigned almost 8,000 German postal codes to either receive fundraising videos or serve as a control group. The study examines changes in donation revenue and frequency, addressing challenges like substitution and measurement issues inherent in studies based on click-through data. The authors find that video fundraising increased donation revenue and frequency for Save the Children during and after the campaign, that the campaign was profitable, and that the effects were similar regardless of video content or impression assignment strategy. They also find evidence of crowding out of donations to other similar charities and projects, and demonstrate that click data may be an inappropriate proxy for donations. The study’s strengths lie in its large-scale geo-randomized design, which circumvents common issues in online advertising research and enhances external validity. The authors preregistered their design and provide robustness checks, additional analyses, and a discussion of profitability. However, the study has some limitations. First, the conclusions are limited to the specific implementation of the campaign. Second, there is a potential for spillovers across postal codes, which may bias the main results downwards. Third, the estimated effects on competing charities are based on data from a subset of charities, and there may be unobserved heterogeneity in the types of projects funded. Fourth, some of the variables are semi-aggregated, which limits the ability to reliably test treatment differences. Finally, while the authors winsorize the data to reduce the influence of outliers, they are unable to do so at the individual level.

Specific issues to address:

  1. Potential Spillovers: The authors acknowledge the potential for spillovers across postal codes, which could bias their main results. While they attempt to address this issue by including a variable indicating the share of treated postal codes within 30 kilometers, this may not fully capture all spillover effects.

  2. Limited Data on Competing Charities: The authors rely on data from a subset of charities to examine the effects of the Save the Children campaign on other organizations. This raises concerns about the representativeness of the data and the potential for unobserved heterogeneity in the types of projects funded.

  3. Semi-Aggregated Variables: The authors acknowledge that some of their variables are semi-aggregated, which limits their ability to reliably test treatment differences. This is a potential limitation of the study’s design.

  4. Winsorizing Data: While the authors winsorize the data to reduce the influence of outliers, they are unable to do so at the individual level. This may not fully address the issue of extreme values in the data.

  5. External Validity: The conclusions are necessarily limited to the specific implementation of the campaign, and it is unclear how the results would generalize to other contexts.

Interference/SUTVA: Geo-randomized Facebook targeting plausibly induces cross-postal-code spillovers and location misclassification; the paper’s neighbor-share regression is suggestive but not a randomized test, so the magnitude/direction of interference remains uncertain and complicates causal estimands.
    1. Treatment intensity vs assignment: Postal-code assignment does not ensure uniform exposure; Facebook’s delivery algorithm can create endogenous within-area intensity and composition, making per-capita effects harder to interpret as “advertising causes X euros per million residents.”
    1. Revenue effects are borderline: Donation revenue results are weaker than frequency (e.g., long-term p<0.1), so ROI/profitability conclusions are sensitive to specification, tail behavior, and aggregation choices.
    1. Winsorization and heavy tails: PLZ-day winsorization at €1,000 may affect inference and ROI in a heavy-tailed donation distribution; robustness is mentioned but should be more fully quantified (e.g., alternative cutoffs, quantile/Poisson models).
    1. Post-period choice and seasonality: Ending outcomes at Dec 31 is substantively motivated but couples treatment persistence to extreme seasonal dynamics; more explicit dynamic/event-study estimates would better separate persistence from seasonal noise.
    1. Competitor/crowding-out measurement mismatch: Competitor datasets are incomplete (often online-only), overlap across sources is unresolved, and sector-wide giving is unobserved, limiting the strength of conclusions about total charitable-sector effects.
    1. Pretreatment imbalance for the 23-charity alliance outcomes: The need for DiD/lagged-outcome adjustment is appropriate, but residual confounding and differing seasonal patterns across areas remain possible; inference is also relatively weak (often p<0.1).
    1. Mechanism claims exceed direct tests: The conclusion that effects primarily reflect the “power of asking” is plausible but not directly isolated from alternative mechanisms (salience, trust, concurrent campaigns/news shocks).
    1. Factorial design interpretation: Differences across video type and impression allocation are mostly not statistically distinguishable; emphasizing “no matter the content, online fundraising works” should be framed as limited power to detect meaningful differences rather than equivalence.
    1. Heterogeneity/multiplicity risk: Many subgroup interactions are reported with strong managerial recommendations, but these appear exploratory and risk false positives without multiplicity control or holdout validation.
    1. Profitability depends on assumptions: Long-run ROI uses an assumed lifetime-value multiplier and implicitly assumes competitor crowd-out does not offset social impact; uncertainty propagation around ROI should be more explicit.
    1. Replication constraints: Although preregistered and well-documented, proprietary and aggregated data plus unclear code availability limit independent reproducibility of key transformations (aggregation, neighbor calculations, data merges).
